You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'mechanism'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'advance_design')
Type: advance_design (survey_experiment). Title: Separating discernment from response bias in machine-label interventions
Question: Does Automated Flagging improve true discernment (sensitivity) rather than just shifting willingness to call posts AI-generated?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes measurement and power. It registers signal-detection outcomes (d′ and criterion) and replicates the one robust arm with an adequate sample.
Design sketch: Arms: Control, Automated Flagging, and Automated Flagging with 80% label accuracy versus 100%, plus a Guide arm as the best-performing education comparator. Respondents judge 40 posts balanced real and AI, with a confidence rating per post. Outcomes are d′, criterion and total accuracy, all registered, with Holm correction across arms. A US online panel with a pre-feed attention check.
Power target: about 230 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (H1 Automated Flagging estimate 0.044, observed SD ~0.13; 80% power for ~0.04 needs ~165 per arm, inflated for Holm correction and the weaker label-accuracy arms); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Individual-level (i-frame) fixes vs system-level (s-frame) change): (a) Cheap individual-level interventions such as labels, nudges and literacy content can measurably improve people's handling of AI-generated media. versus (b) Individual-level levers yield small, inconsistent effects, and meaningful change needs system-level measures such as platform-level or provenance infrastructure.. The source study says: Leans to b for educational and mindfulness-type interventions: pooled accuracy +1.0 point (p=0.132), with several arms null or harmful. Automated Flagging (+4.4), a system-supplied label, is the clearest gain, which weakly fits the s-frame view. The study cannot test system-level effects.

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a survey experiment on a US online panel (fielded October to November 2023) in which respondents were randomised to a control or one of 11 interventions before a feed-based discernment task. The analysis sample was 2,030 of 2,257 respondents. Four registered outcomes were total accuracy, attitudes toward AI, confidence in AI detection and trust in online information. Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]), while Mindfulness lowered it by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). The AI Literacy Guide estimate (4.7 points, 95% CI [0.2, 9.2]) was borderline and uncorrected for multiple tests. Pooled across arms, accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, SE 0.7, p = 0.132). Some arms lowered attitudes toward AI or confidence in detection. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons and several arms were small, so isolated effects should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; pooled across 11 arms, accuracy was 1.0 point higher (SE 0.7, p = 0.132), not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p = 0.004). The AI Literacy Guide estimate (4.7 points) is borderline and uncorrected (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Two arms lowered confidence in AI detection, and one (Inoculation) raised it.
- Exploratory (post hoc): Breathing Exercise and the AI Accuracy Nudge raised detection of AI-generated posts, but these tests were not planned.
- Caveat: 44 registered arm-level tests were run with no multiplicity correction, and several arms are small (under 100), so isolated significant results may be chance.

Limitations: The study ran 44 arm-level tests on registered outcomes and 22 more post hoc, with no correction for multiple comparisons, so some of the significant results are probably chance. Several arms are small, notably Inoculation (78) and the two AI Literacy Infographics (about 80–100), which limits precision. Some data were collected before registration, though later batches followed the plan. The panel is a US online sample, so the results may not generalise. Outcomes were measured right after the intervention, so durability is unknown. Detection of AI-generated posts and recognition of authentic posts were not registered, and the Breathing Exercise and Flagging patterns across outcomes are hard to interpret.

function.description: Hand a structured result to the orchestrator. Set final=true when your task is complete.

value.title: Separating discernment from response bias in machine-label interventions
value.rationale: Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004), but accuracy cannot show whether labels improved sensitivity or merely shifted willingness to say AI; detection and real-content accuracy were not registered. With 44 uncorrected tests and small arms, the effect also needs replication with adequate power.
value.contribution: Decomposes the label effect into d-prime and criterion and tests whether label accuracy matters, bearing on whether a system-supplied cue beats individual-level education.
limitations: Simulated labels are not a real platform-level system
Guide arm is a single education comparator

design.title: Separating discernment from response bias in machine-label interventions
design.overview: Respondents are randomised to Control, Automated Flagging (100% accurate labels), Automated Flagging at 80% accuracy, or the AI Literacy Guide. They judge 40 posts (20 real, 20 AI) and rate confidence in each. Signal-detection d-prime and criterion are computed per person.
design.hypothesis: H1: Automated Flagging raises d-prime relative to control (not only a criterion shift). H2: 80%-accurate labels yield a smaller d-prime gain than 100%-accurate labels. H3: The Guide raises d-prime less than Automated Flagging.
design.primaryOutcome: d-prime (sensitivity) from 40 judgments, with criterion and total accuracy as co-registered outcomes.
design.comparison: Each treatment arm vs Control on d-prime, criterion and accuracy with Holm correction across arms; Flagging 100% vs 80% and Flagging vs Guide as planned contrasts. Report pooled and arm-level SEs and CIs.
design.population: US adults on an online panel, passing a pre-feed attention check.

conditions.title: Automated Flagging 100%
conditions.description: Posts carry machine-learning detection labels that are always correct.

conditions.title: Automated Flagging 80%
conditions.description: Posts carry detection labels that are correct for 80% of posts.

conditions.title: AI Literacy Guide
conditions.description: A comprehensive guide with examples of AI artifacts in images and videos.

questions.text: You are invited to a research study on how people judge online media. It takes about 10 minutes and is voluntary. Do you consent to participate?

People are very busy these days and many do not have time to follow what goes on in the government. We are testing whether people read questions. To show that you've read this much, answer both "extremely interested" and "very interested."
In the next section, each post will carry a label from an automated AI-detection system stating whether it is likely AI-generated or likely real. Labels may not always be right.

Please read this guide. It explains common artifacts in AI-generated images and videos, such as distorted hands, inconsistent lighting, garbled text, unnatural textures and odd motion, with side-by-side examples. Take your time before continuing.

You will now see 40 posts, some real and some AI-generated. For each, mark whether it is AI-generated and rate your confidence. If unsure, go with your gut. Posts are shown in random order, and the system supplies labels where applicable.
For each of the 40 posts shown (images and videos, 20 real and 20 AI-generated), is the post AI-generated?
How confident are you in each judgment?
I feel confident in my ability to detect artificial intelligence.

Thank you. This study examined whether labels and education help people identify AI-generated media. Some labels shown were deliberately inaccurate, and some posts were AI-generated. Please do not rely on the labels you saw.

assumptions: Target about 230 per arm (about 920 total) to detect 0.03 at 80% power; H1 Automated Flagging estimate 0.044, observed SD about 0.13; 80% power for about 0.04 needs about 165 per arm, inflated for Holm correction and the weaker 80% label arm.
The matrix shows 5 sample rows; the deployed task presents all 40 posts one per page with the same two questions each.
d-prime uses a log-linear correction for extreme hit and false-alarm rates; AI-generated is the signal.
US online panel; compensation per panel standard.
unresolved: The 40 real and AI-generated post media files and the label assignment for the 80% arm must be supplied by the research team.
IRB approval number and compensation amount.

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'boundary'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'generalizability_conditional')
Type: generalizability_conditional (survey_experiment). Title: Does the label effect hold for newer generators and low-trust respondents?
Question: Does the Automated Flagging gain persist across stimulus realism (older vs current-generation synthetic media) and baseline media trust?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes sample and stimulus limits: the 2023 stimuli and US panel may not generalise, and the pooled null may hide moderation.
Design sketch: Control vs Automated Flagging, with the post set randomised between 2023-era and current-generation synthetic images and video. Media trust and AI familiarity are measured pre-treatment and used as registered moderators. Outcomes are accuracy and d′, with a re-contact two weeks later for durability on a subsample.
Moderator or condition whose variation the design must cover: Generator realism (2023 vs current) and baseline media trust (pre-registered median split)
Power target: about 350 per arm to detect 0.04 at 80% power (Interaction effects need roughly 4x the n of the main effect 0.044; MDE for the 0.0318–0.042 range in H1); record it in design.assumptions

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a survey experiment on a US online panel (fielded October to November 2023) in which respondents were randomised to a control or one of 11 interventions before a feed-based discernment task. The analysis sample was 2,030 of 2,257 respondents. Four registered outcomes were total accuracy, attitudes toward AI, confidence in AI detection and trust in online information. Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]), while Mindfulness lowered it by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). The AI Literacy Guide estimate (4.7 points, 95% CI [0.2, 9.2]) was borderline and uncorrected for multiple tests. Pooled across arms, accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, SE 0.7, p = 0.132). Some arms lowered attitudes toward AI or confidence in detection. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons and several arms were small, so isolated effects should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; pooled across 11 arms, accuracy was 1.0 point higher (SE 0.7, p = 0.132), not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p = 0.004). The AI Literacy Guide estimate (4.7 points) is borderline and uncorrected (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Two arms lowered confidence in AI detection, and one (Inoculation) raised it.
- Exploratory (post hoc): Breathing Exercise and the AI Accuracy Nudge raised detection of AI-generated posts, but these tests were not planned.
- Caveat: 44 registered arm-level tests were run with no multiplicity correction, and several arms are small (under 100), so isolated significant results may be chance.

Limitations: The study ran 44 arm-level tests on registered outcomes and 22 more post hoc, with no correction for multiple comparisons, so some of the significant results are probably chance. Several arms are small, notably Inoculation (78) and the two AI Literacy Infographics (about 80–100), which limits precision. Some data were collected before registration, though later batches followed the plan. The panel is a US online sample, so the results may not generalise. Outcomes were measured right after the intervention, so durability is unknown. Detection of AI-generated posts and recognition of authentic posts were not registered, and the Breathing Exercise and Flagging patterns across outcomes are hard to interpret.

function.description: Hand a structured result to the orchestrator. Set final=true when your task is complete.

value.title: Does the label effect hold for newer generators and low-trust respondents?
value.rationale: Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p = 0.004) but the pooled effect across 11 arms was only +1.0 (SE 0.7), and stimuli were 2023-era with a US panel. Realism of current generators and baseline media trust may moderate the label effect, and durability was never measured.
value.contribution: Tests whether the Automated Flagging gain generalises across generator realism and baseline media trust and persists two weeks later.
limitations: Interaction tests need large samples; the median split loses power.
Current-generation stimuli must be sourced and verified by the research team.
Re-contact attrition may bias the durability subsample.

design.title: Automated Flagging across generator realism and media trust
design.overview: Respondents report media trust and AI familiarity, then are randomised to Control or Automated Flagging. Each also sees a feed of posts randomly drawn from either a 2023-era or a current-generation synthetic set (mixed with authentic posts). They judge each post AI or real. A subsample is re-contacted two weeks later.
design.hypothesis: H1: Automated Flagging raises accuracy and d-prime relative to control. H2: The gain is smaller for current-generation stimuli. H3: The gain differs between low and high baseline media trust (median split, pre-registered).
design.primaryOutcome: Accuracy (share of posts judged correctly) and d-prime
design.comparison: Automated Flagging vs Control, crossed with stimulus set (2023 vs current) and median-split media trust; interactions are the focal tests.
design.population: US online panel adults, about 1,400 per stimulus set crossed design; quota sampled on age, gender and education.

assumptions: Power: about 350 per arm per cell to detect 0.04 at 80% power; interactions need roughly 4x the n of the main effect 0.044, with MDE in the 0.0318-0.042 range from H1.
Panel: US online panel, about 10 minutes; 24 posts per respondent, repeated in the feed pattern of the source with one post shown per page.
Media trust median split is pre-registered; AI familiarity is a secondary moderator.
Durability: re-contact about 2 weeks later on a subsample of roughly 30%, with a new post set; d-prime computed from hit and false alarm rates with log-linear correction.
The post embedded nodes stand for a repeated feed of 24 posts; the research team loads the full set.
unresolved: Current-generation synthetic images and video and matched authentic posts must be produced by the research team.
Compensation, IRB number and the re-contact wave instrument are to be supplied by the research team.
Exact label accuracy for Automated Flagging must match the source study.

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. ## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'theoretical_debate')
Type: theoretical_debate (survey_experiment). Title: Individual literacy vs system-supplied cue: which carries the effect?
Question: Is the accuracy gain from machine labels due to external information (s-frame) or to changed individual vigilance (i-frame)?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes design confounding: it separates cue content from attention or priming effects, which the original arms bundled.
Design sketch: 2x2 between-subjects: label present or absent, crossed with literacy training (Guide) present or absent, plus a placebo-label arm showing uninformative labels. If gain comes only with real labels, the s-frame reading is supported; if training alone or the placebo helps, vigilance explains it. Outcomes are accuracy and d′ on 40 posts.
Power target: about 300 per arm to detect 0.033 at 80% power (H1 MDE for n≈290 vs 181 arms was 0.034; interaction contrast needs the larger cells); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Individual-level (i-frame) fixes vs system-level (s-frame) change): (a) Cheap individual-level interventions such as labels, nudges and literacy content can measurably improve people's handling of AI-generated media. versus (b) Individual-level levers yield small, inconsistent effects, and meaningful change needs system-level measures such as platform-level or provenance infrastructure.. The source study says: Leans to b for educational and mindfulness-type interventions: pooled accuracy +1.0 point (p=0.132), with several arms null or harmful. Automated Flagging (+4.4), a system-supplied label, is the clearest gain, which weakly fits the s-frame view. The study cannot test system-level effects.

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a survey experiment on a US online panel (fielded October to November 2023) in which respondents were randomised to a control or one of 11 interventions before a feed-based discernment task. The analysis sample was 2,030 of 2,257 respondents. Four registered outcomes were total accuracy, attitudes toward AI, confidence in AI detection and trust in online information. Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]), while Mindfulness lowered it by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). The AI Literacy Guide estimate (4.7 points, 95% CI [0.2, 9.2]) was borderline and uncorrected for multiple tests. Pooled across arms, accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, SE 0.7, p = 0.132). Some arms lowered attitudes toward AI or confidence in detection. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons and several arms were small, so isolated effects should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; pooled across 11 arms, accuracy was 1.0 point higher (SE 0.7, p = 0.132), not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p = 0.004). The AI Literacy Guide estimate (4.7 points) is borderline and uncorrected (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Two arms lowered confidence in AI detection, and one (Inoculation) raised it.
- Exploratory (post hoc): Breathing Exercise and the AI Accuracy Nudge raised detection of AI-generated posts, but these tests were not planned.
- Caveat: 44 registered arm-level tests were run with no multiplicity correction, and several arms are small (under 100), so isolated significant results may be chance.

Limitations: The study ran 44 arm-level tests on registered outcomes and 22 more post hoc, with no correction for multiple comparisons, so some of the significant results are probably chance. Several arms are small, notably Inoculation (78) and the two AI Literacy Infographics (about 80–100), which limits precision. Some data were collected before registration, though later batches followed the plan. The panel is a US online sample, so the results may not generalise. Outcomes were measured right after the intervention, so durability is unknown. Detection of AI-generated posts and recognition of authentic posts were not registered, and the Breathing Exercise and Flagging patterns across outcomes are hard to interpret.

design.title: Label vs literacy training: 2x2 plus placebo label
design.overview: Respondents are randomised to one of five arms: control, real label only, Guide only, real label plus Guide, or placebo label. All see the same 40-post feed and judge each post as AI-generated or authentic. Accuracy and d-prime are computed from the judgments.
design.hypothesis: H1 (s-frame): real labels raise accuracy and d-prime, and the Guide alone and the placebo label do not. H2 (i-frame): the Guide alone or the placebo label raises accuracy and d-prime comparably to real labels. H3: the label x Guide interaction is positive if training makes labels more useful.
design.primaryOutcome: Accuracy: share of 40 posts judged correctly, with d-prime as a co-primary outcome.
design.comparison: Real label vs control; Guide vs control; placebo vs control; real label vs placebo; label x Guide interaction in the 2x2 cells (control, label, Guide, label plus Guide).
design.population: US adults on an online panel, about 300 per arm (1,500 total).

questions.text: You are invited to take part in a research study about how people judge online media. It takes about 10 minutes and participation is voluntary. Do you consent to participate?
In general, how much trust and confidence do you have in the news media when it comes to reporting the news fully, accurately and fairly?

Please read this guide on how to spot AI-generated images and videos. It describes common artifacts such as distorted hands, inconsistent lighting, garbled text and unnatural motion, with examples. Take your time; you will then view a feed of posts.
Next you will see 40 posts. For each, mark whether it is AI-generated or authentic. If you are unsure, go with your gut.

Each post in the feed carries a label from an automated AI-detection system, which is accurate about 80% of the time. [IMAGE: example feed post with a detection label reading 'Likely AI-generated' or 'Likely authentic']. For each of the 40 posts, mark whether it is AI-generated or authentic.

Each post in the feed carries a label from an automated system showing a random content category. [IMAGE: example feed post with a label reading 'Category: Lifestyle' or 'Category: Entertainment', unrelated to AI status]. For each of the 40 posts, mark whether it is AI-generated or authentic.
[IMAGE: example feed post with no label]. For each of the 40 posts, mark whether it is AI-generated or authentic.
I feel confident in my ability to detect artificial intelligence.
How much did you rely on labels or tips rather than your own inspection of each post?
Thank you. This study tested what helps people recognise AI-generated media. Some labels shown were uninformative or only partly accurate by design. Your quiz score reflects your answers only.

assumptions: Power: about 300 per arm to detect 0.033 at 80% power; the source H1 MDE was 0.034 for n≈290 vs 181 arms, and the interaction contrast needs the larger cells. Total about 1,500.
Accuracy and d-prime are computed from the 40 post-level judgments, with 20 AI-generated and 20 authentic posts.
Real labels are about 80% accurate, matching a realistic detector.
Platform: online panel, about 10 minutes. Compensation follows panel norms.
Report pooled SEs and CIs for contrasts, and correct for the few planned comparisons.
unresolved: The 40 post media files and their ground-truth labels must be supplied by the research team.
The Guide content and the real and placebo label assets must be produced.
IRB number and compensation are to be supplied.

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'alternative'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'theoretical_debate')
Type: theoretical_debate (survey_experiment). Title: Individual literacy vs system-supplied cue: which carries the effect?
Question: Is the accuracy gain from machine labels due to external information (s-frame) or to changed individual vigilance (i-frame)?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes design confounding: it separates cue content from attention or priming effects, which the original arms bundled.
Design sketch: 2x2 between-subjects: label present or absent, crossed with literacy training (Guide) present or absent, plus a placebo-label arm showing uninformative labels. If gain comes only with real labels, the s-frame reading is supported; if training alone or the placebo helps, vigilance explains it. Outcomes are accuracy and d′ on 40 posts.
Power target: about 300 per arm to detect 0.033 at 80% power (H1 MDE for n≈290 vs 181 arms was 0.034; interaction contrast needs the larger cells); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Individual-level (i-frame) fixes vs system-level (s-frame) change): (a) Cheap individual-level interventions such as labels, nudges and literacy content can measurably improve people's handling of AI-generated media. versus (b) Individual-level levers yield small, inconsistent effects, and meaningful change needs system-level measures such as platform-level or provenance infrastructure.. The source study says: Leans to b for educational and mindfulness-type interventions: pooled accuracy +1.0 point (p=0.132), with several arms null or harmful. Automated Flagging (+4.4), a system-supplied label, is the clearest gain, which weakly fits the s-frame view. The study cannot test system-level effects.

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a survey experiment on a US online panel (fielded October to November 2023) in which respondents were randomised to a control or one of 11 interventions before a feed-based discernment task. The analysis sample was 2,030 of 2,257 respondents. Four registered outcomes were total accuracy, attitudes toward AI, confidence in AI detection and trust in online information. Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]), while Mindfulness lowered it by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). The AI Literacy Guide estimate (4.7 points, 95% CI [0.2, 9.2]) was borderline and uncorrected for multiple tests. Pooled across arms, accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, SE 0.7, p = 0.132). Some arms lowered attitudes toward AI or confidence in detection. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons and several arms were small, so isolated effects should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; pooled across 11 arms, accuracy was 1.0 point higher (SE 0.7, p = 0.132), not distinguishable from zero.
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p = 0.004). The AI Literacy Guide estimate (4.7 points) is borderline and uncorrected (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Two arms lowered confidence in AI detection, and one (Inoculation) raised it.
- Exploratory (post hoc): Breathing Exercise and the AI Accuracy Nudge raised detection of AI-generated posts, but these tests were not planned.
- Caveat: 44 registered arm-level tests were run with no multiplicity correction, and several arms are small (under 100), so isolated significant results may be chance.

Limitations: The study ran 44 arm-level tests on registered outcomes and 22 more post hoc, with no correction for multiple comparisons, so some of the significant results are probably chance. Several arms are small, notably Inoculation (78) and the two AI Literacy Infographics (about 80–100), which limits precision. Some data were collected before registration, though later batches followed the plan. The panel is a US online sample, so the results may not generalise. Outcomes were measured right after the intervention, so durability is unknown. Detection of AI-generated posts and recognition of authentic posts were not registered, and the Breathing Exercise and Flagging patterns across outcomes are hard to interpret.

value.title: Individual literacy vs system-supplied cue: which carries the effect?
value.rationale: In the source study, Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]) and the AI Literacy Guide by 4.7 points (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]), while pooled accuracy was only +1.0 point (SE 0.7, p=0.132). The original arms bundled cue content with attention and priming, so it is unclear whether the gain comes from external information (s-frame) or changed vigilance (i-frame).
value.contribution: Separates the information content of a machine label from vigilance and priming effects, using a 2x2 design plus a placebo-label arm.
limitations: Outcomes are measured immediately, so durability is unknown.
The placebo label may be read as a real cue.
Platform-level systemic change is still not tested, only a system-supplied cue.
The 5-arm layout is not a full factorial. The placebo arm has no crossed Guide cell.

design.title: Label vs literacy training: 2x2 plus placebo label
design.overview: Respondents are randomised to one of five arms: control, real label only, Guide only, real label plus Guide, or placebo label. All see the same 40-post feed and judge each post as AI-generated or authentic. Accuracy and d-prime are computed from the judgments.
design.hypothesis: H1 (s-frame): real labels raise accuracy and d-prime, while the Guide alone and the placebo label do not. H2 (i-frame): the Guide alone or the placebo label raises accuracy and d-prime comparably to real labels. H3: the label x Guide interaction is positive if training makes labels more useful.
design.primaryOutcome: Accuracy: share of 40 posts judged correctly, with d-prime as a co-primary outcome.
design.comparison: Real label vs control; Guide vs control; placebo vs control; real label vs placebo; label x Guide interaction in the 2x2 cells (control, label, Guide, label plus Guide).
design.population: US adults on an online panel, about 300 per arm (1,500 total).

conditions.title: Guide only
conditions.description: AI Literacy Guide before the feed, no labels.

conditions.title: Label plus Guide
conditions.description: Guide before the feed and real labels on posts.

conditions.title: Placebo label
conditions.description: Posts carry uninformative labels unrelated to AI status.

questions.text: You are invited to take part in a research study about how people judge online media. It takes about 10 minutes and participation is voluntary. Do you consent to participate?
In general, how much trust and confidence do you have in the news media when it comes to reporting the news fully, accurately and fairly?

Please read this guide on how to spot AI-generated images and videos. It describes common artifacts such as distorted hands, inconsistent lighting, garbled text and unnatural motion, with examples. Take your time; you will then view a feed of posts.

Next you will see 40 posts. Each post carries a label from an automated AI-detection system, which is accurate about 80% of the time. [IMAGE: example feed post with a detection label reading 'Likely AI-generated' or 'Likely authentic']. For each of the 40 posts, mark whether it is AI-generated or authentic.

Next you will see 40 posts. Each post carries a label from an automated system showing a content category. [IMAGE: example feed post with a label reading 'Category: Lifestyle' or 'Category: Entertainment']. For each of the 40 posts, mark whether it is AI-generated or authentic.
Next you will see 40 posts. [IMAGE: example feed post with no label]. For each of the 40 posts, mark whether it is AI-generated or authentic. If you are unsure, go with your gut.
I feel confident in my ability to detect artificial intelligence.
How much did you rely on labels or tips rather than your own inspection of each post?
Thank you. This study tested what helps people recognise AI-generated media. Some labels shown were uninformative or only partly accurate by design. Your quiz score reflects your answers only.

assumptions: Power: about 300 per arm to detect 0.033 at 80% power; the source H1 MDE was 0.034 for n≈290 vs 181 arms, and the interaction contrast needs the larger cells. Total about 1,500.
Accuracy and d-prime are computed from the 40 post-level judgments, with 20 AI-generated and 20 authentic posts.
Real labels are about 80% accurate, matching a realistic detector.
Platform: online panel, about 10 minutes. Compensation follows panel norms.
Report pooled SEs and CIs for contrasts, and correct for the few planned comparisons.
unresolved: The 40 post media files and their ground-truth labels must be supplied by the research team.
The Guide content and the real and placebo label assets must be produced.
IRB number and compensation are to be supplied.
